# Min-Plus Convolution Lower Bounds via a Higher-Order BSG Theorem

**Authors:** Nick Fischer Note: Max Planck Institute for Informatics. E-Mail: nfischer@mpi-inf.mpg.de Ce Jin Note: University of California, Berkeley. E-Mail: cejin@berkeley.edu Yinzhan Xu Note: University of California, San Diego. E-Mail: xyzhan@ucsd.edu

## Abstract

Min-Plus Convolution is a central problem in fine-grained complexity, and the associated Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis forms the basis for a wide range of conditional lower bounds for fundamental problems. It is closely connected to the APSP and 3SUM Hypotheses, and in fact implies both, making it a unifying hypothesis for two of the main pillars of the area. In this work we establish several strong results related to Min-Plus Convolution. We design a universe reduction, showing, under a plausible additive combinatorics assumption, that the Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis is equivalent to the Strong Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis. We also obtain tight conditional lower bounds for multiple long-standing problems, including Min-Max Convolution and Bounded Monotone Min-Plus Convolution.

Our approach is inspired by Fischer’s recent equivalence between several variants of APSP [STOC ’26], but extending that technique to the arithmetic setting requires overcoming deep obstacles. To this end, we develop a novel additive structure theorem that can be viewed as a higher-order substitute of the Balog–Szemerédi–Gowers (BSG) theorem, allowing us to extract strong additive structure even from weakly structured sets. Building on this structural result, we show that certain structured 3SUM instances (namely, sets with low rank) can be solved in truly subquadratic time. This algorithm forms the main algorithmic ingredient in our reductions. Besides, it generalizes all previously known truly subquadratic-time special cases of 3SUM, and is therefore of independent interest.

## 1 Introduction

The Min-Plus Convolution problem is one of the central problems in fine-grained complexity. Given two integer sequences $A$ and $B$ of length $n$ , the task is to compute the sequence $A*B$ where $(A*B)[k]=\min_{i}(A[i]+B[k-i])$ . Naively this takes time $O(n^{2})$ , and the fastest known algorithm achieves only mild improvements, $n^{2}/2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}$ [54]. This leads to the Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis [31, 45] postulating that truly subquadratic time $O(n^{2-\epsilon})$ , for some constant $\epsilon>0$ , is impossible.11 1 Unless otherwise specified, the entry bounds of all problems we consider are polynomially bounded in the input size. The postulated lower bounds hold in the Word-RAM model with $\Theta(\log n)$ -bit words, and hold against potentially randomized algorithms. This hypothesis has been used to establish conditional lower bounds for problems including Knapsack [31, 45], Unbounded Subset Sum and the Frobenius problem [42], Integer Programming [39], Tree Sparsity [7], hop-bounded shortest paths [43, 53], and an approximate version of 3SUM [16].

Beyond its many applications, the Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis plays a central conceptual role in the landscape of fine-grained complexity. It is closely connected to the famous 3SUM and APSP Hypotheses, and in fact implies them both [11, 7]. Thus, it can be viewed as a unified hypothesis of two of the main pillars of the area. In particular, the Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis is one of the strongest well-established hypotheses, implying more conditional lower bounds than most other fine-grained assumptions. This makes studying Min-Plus Convolution a fundamental problem in its own right.

In this work, we establish several strong results that significantly sharpen our understanding of Min-Plus Convolution. We design a universe reduction: assuming a plausible hypothesis from additive combinatorics, we show that the Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis is equivalent to its strong variant, which asserts hardness even for instances with integer weights bounded by $O(n)$ . As a consequence, we obtain tight conditional lower bounds for a variety of long-standing convolution problems with “intermediate” complexity, including Min-Max Convolution and Bounded Monotone Min-Plus Convolution.

### 1.1 Starting Point

Our starting point is a recent breakthrough by Fischer [36], which establishes analogous results for the APSP problem. Specifically, Fischer shows that the APSP Hypothesis and the Strong APSP Hypothesis are equivalent, assuming a plausible hypothesis from additive combinatorics and that $\omega=2$ . He further shows that the Directed Unweighted APSP Hypothesis, stating that APSP in unweighted directed graphs requires $n^{2.5-o(1)}$ time, is in this equivalence class. This greatly sharpens our understanding of the role of the universe size in APSP.

Given that Min-Plus Convolution and APSP are similar in many ways, one might wonder whether Fischer’s technique transfers. In particular, can it be applied to show the equivalence between the Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis and the Strong Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis?

At a high level, Fischer [36] follows a structure-versus-random approach that could, in principle, apply to any problem $P$ , and that has already been successful in other fine-grained reductions [2, 1, 40, 26]. It can be summarized in three generic steps:

- (1) Identify a suitable measure of structure for $P$ .

- (2) Show that $P$ can be solved fast on structured instances.

- (3) Then, suppose that we aim to design a fine-grained reduction from $P$ to some other problem $Q$ . Given any instance of $P$ , we first repeatedly extract structured subinstances, and solve these subinstances with the fast algorithm from step 2. Once there is no more structured subinstance, we regard the remaining instance as pseudo-random, and exploit the pseudo-randomness in the reduction to $Q$ .

Of course, successfully implementing this approach hinges crucially on the choice of the structure notion. It has to be weak enough so that structured instances can be solved efficiently, but strong enough so that the corresponding pseudo-random instances can be exploited in the reduction.

In Fischer’s setup, $P$ is the APSP problem (or rather, for technical reasons, the equivalent Min-Plus Product problem), and the relevant notion of structure is a matrix rank parameter known as select-plus rank22 2 The select-plus rank of an $n\times n$ integer matrix $A$ is the smallest number $r$ such that there exist matrices $U,V$ of sizes $n\times r$ and $r\times n$ , respectively, so that $A[i,j]\in\bigcup_{k=1}^{r}\{U[i,k]+V[k,j]\}$ .. A major technical contribution is a fast algorithm for instances of low rank, from which the universe reduction and further lower bounds follow via the general framework.

Let us return to Min-Plus Convolution. As the analogy to Min-Plus Product is strong, a priori one may hope that Fischer’s techniques can be extended to Min-Plus Convolution without too much difficulty. However, our situation is quite the exception. Obtaining the analogous results for Min-Plus Convolution poses several substantially new obstacles that are not present in the matrix world. First, it is entirely unclear what the appropriate notion of structure should be for sequences or sets. This naturally falls into the realm of additive combinatorics; however, any such notion must capture extremely weak additive structure, far from the commonly used strong structure measures. This leads to a second major challenge: the existing tools from additive combinatorics are not well suited for this regime, and we need to invent our own structural results. All in all, our route involves three steps, each of which is interesting in its own right:

- • We develop a new additive structure theorem that can be viewed as a “higher-order” substitute of the Balog–Szemerédi–Gowers theorem (Section 1.2).

- • We then identify the appropriate structure notion, called rank in analogy to [36], and show that low-rank instances of Min-Plus Convolution can be solved in subquadratic time, based on the new structure theorem. In fact, we directly work with the harder 3SUM problem (Section 1.3).

- • Equipped with this new algorithm, we derive the aforementioned universe reduction and strong lower bounds from Min-Plus Convolution in analogy to Fischer’s proof (Sections 1.4 and 1.5).

### 1.2 A New Additive Structure Theorem

Using additive combinatorics in fine-grained algorithm design and complexity is an exciting recent trend [25, 20, 18, 19, 1, 40, 26, 41, 21, 27, 15, 33, 3, 29, 36]. This was pioneered by Chan and Lewenstein [25], who introduced the celebrated Balog–Szemerédi–Gowers (BSG) Theorem to our community, and derived various strong algorithmic consequences of it. The BSG Theorem has since found many more applications [25, 1, 40, 26, 33, 3], notably also in Fischer’s work [36], and became an important part of the fine-grained toolkit. To understand both the strengths and the limitations of the BSG Theorem—and how we overcome them—let us take a short excursus into additive combinatorics.

Intuitively, the BSG theorem states that any set $A$ with a lot of “local structure”, e.g., in the form of many solutions to the equation $a_{1}+a_{2}=a_{3}+a_{4}$ for $a_{1},a_{2},a_{3},a_{4}\in A$ , must admit a large subset $H$ that is “globally structured”, in the sense that the sumset $H+H=\{a+b:a,b\in H\}$ is small. Such sets $H$ are also called low-doubling sets since their doubling $\frac{|H+H|}{|H|}$ is small. To state the BSG Theorem quantitatively, let us introduce a piece of notation that will turn out convenient later:

$$ \Pop^{k}(A;p)=\left\{x:\lvert\{(a_{1},\dots,a_{k})\in A^{k}:x=a_{1}+\dots+a_{k}\}\rvert\geq p\right\}, $$

i.e., the set of all sums $a_{1}+\dots+a_{k}$ that can be expressed in at least $p$ distinct ways. We refer to these as the popular $k$ -sums. Then the BSG theorem can be equivalently stated in the following (non-standard) form:33 3 To relate Theorem 1.1 to the usual BSG Theorem (e.g., Theorem 2.3), note that $A$ has a popular 4-sum, $\Pop^{4}(A;|A|^{3}/K)\neq\emptyset$ , if and only if $A$ has large additive energy, $E(A)\geq|A|^{3}/K^{\prime}$ , where $K$ and $K^{\prime}$ depend polynomially on each other. The “if” direction is immediate by Cauchy–Schwarz. The “only if” direction follows from some basic Fourier analysis and Hölder’s inequality (see e.g., [40, Lemma 2.11]).

#### 1.1BSG Theorem, Reformulated.

Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{Z}$ be a set with $\Pop^{4}(A;|A|^{3}/K)\neq\emptyset$ . Then there is a set $H\subseteq\mathbb{Z}$ satisfying that:

- • $|H|\leq|A|$ (in fact, we can take $H$ as a subset of $A$ ),

- • $|H+H|\leq K^{O(1)}|H|$ ,

- • $|A\cap H|\geq|A|/K^{O(1)}$ .

In other words, the existence of a popular 4-sum certifies the presence of a large low-doubling subset.

Unfortunately, the BSG Theorem is insufficient to deal with sets exhibiting much weaker additive structure. Consider the following example. Let $A$ be a random size- $n$ set in a large universe $\{0,\dots,u\}$ , say for $u=n^{10}$ . In this case, with good probability, each 4-sum is unique. In particular, there are no popular 4-sums. This is consistent with the fact that $A$ contains no large low-doubling subset. Nevertheless, $A$ is not entirely unstructured: it is contained in a much larger low-doubling set, namely the entire universe $\{0,\dots,u\}$ . The challenge is that this weak global structure is invisible to the 4-sums. Our key insight is that such weak structure can be detected by moving to larger $k$ -sums. Specifically, we show that for sufficiently large $k$ , the presence of a popular $k$ -sum reveals the desired structure. This leads to the following higher-order analogue of the BSG Theorem.

#### 1.2Popular $k$ -Sums Imply Low-Doubling Structure.

For every $c>0$ and $\epsilon>0$ , there is some $k=k(c,\epsilon)$ such that the following holds. Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{Z}$ and assume that $\Pop^{k}(A;p)\neq\emptyset$ for some $p=\Omega(|A|^{k-1-c})$ . Then there exists a set $H\subseteq\mathbb{Z}$ and some $K=O_{c,\epsilon}(|A|^{\epsilon})$ such that:

- • $|H|\leq K|A|^{1+c}$ ,

- • $|H+H|\leq K|H|$ ,

- • $|A\cap H|\geq|A|/K$ .

To illustrate how to apply the theorem, consider again the example from before. We apply Theorem 1.2 with $c=9$ , and for some arbitrarily small constant $\epsilon$ . The theorem then chooses some constant $k=k(c,\epsilon)$ . There is indeed some $k$ -sum in $A$ that is $\Omega(|A|^{k-1-c})$ -popular (as there are $|A|^{k}$ $k$ -sums taking at most $k|A|^{10}$ distinct values), satisfying the premise of the theorem. Theorem 1.2 then implies that a large part of $A$ is contained in some set $H$ of size at most $K|A|^{10}$ and doubling $|H+H|\leq K|H|$ . Here, the doubling $K=O_{c,\epsilon}(|A|^{\epsilon})$ is controlled by the initial choice of $\epsilon$ . I.e., we can force $H$ to be arbitrarily well-structured (as long as $K$ is polynomially large), at the only cost of increasing the constant $k$ . Theorem 1.2 turns out to be a surprisingly powerful tool that is likely to find more applications beyond our specific interest related to the Min-Plus Convolution problem.

The proof of Theorem 1.2 builds on the asymmetric BSG Theorem of Tao and Vu [52], a significantly more intricate extension of BSG to pairs of sets of different sizes. In fact, our result is the first in fine-grained complexity, and even theoretical computer science as a whole, that exploits the asymmetric BSG Theorem, to our knowledge.

At a very high level, the proof of Theorem 1.2 is by increasing $k$ gradually and tracking the sets of popular $\ell$ -sums for $\ell=4,5,\dots,k$ . By a pigeonhole argument, at some point, the popular $\ell$ -sums and $(\ell+1)$ -sums correlate (both in size and structurally), at which point the asymmetric BSG theorem can be applied to extract the desired low-doubling set. We provide a detailed proof in Section 3. We also face the extra challenge that for our algorithmic applications, it does not suffice to know that $H$ exists, but we must be able to compute $H$ . Therefore, along the way we also devise an efficient randomized algorithm to find $H$ as in Theorem 1.2 (see Theorem 3.5). Notably, to this end we also had to design an efficient algorithm for the asymmetric BSG Theorem (see Section 7). This black box will certainly be handy for other algorithms in the future.

Finally, let us remark that there are some other higher-order variants of BSG that have been studied in additive combinatorics [51, 10, 50, 46]. However, unfortunately none of these existing results applies in the weakly structured regime required for our applications (though some of the same ideas, e.g. as in [9, 50], turn out useful for the proof of Theorem 1.2 as well). This concludes our additive combinatorics excursus.

### 1.3 Low-Rank 3SUM

Equipped with Theorem 1.2 we are now in a position to start implementing the structure-versus-randomness approach following Fischer [36]. Recall from before that the foundation of Fischer’s proof is to identify a certain rank parameter, and to design a truly subcubic-time algorithm for computing the min-plus product of low-rank matrices. An immediate challenge of extending Fischer’s proof to Min-Plus Convolution is the lack of such a rank notion. It is unclear what should be the rank of a sequence or a set with respect to normal convolutions, let alone Min-Plus Convolution.

A main contribution of our paper is to identify a suitable notion of rank for sequences, which is strong enough (so that unstructured instances are sufficiently pseudo-random to complete our reductions) but not overpowering (so we can still design a fast algorithm for Min-Plus Convolution on low-rank sequences).

In fact, we will directly work with 3SUM, a harder problem than Min-Plus Convolution. Given three sets $A,B,C$ , it asks to decide if there is a solution to $a+b=c$ for $a\in A,b\in B,c\in C$ . 3SUM can be solved naively in time $O(n^{2})$ , and the 3SUM Hypothesis speculates that it cannot be solved in truly subquadratic time. This hypothesis is among the “three big” fine-grained assumptions. As mentioned before, Min-Plus Convolution reduces tightly to 3SUM, and for this reason we prove a stronger statement by showing that low-rank 3SUM is in subquadratic time. Another advantage is that the structure measure can be defined for sets rather than sequences, which turns out cleaner:

#### 1.3Rank.

The rank of a set $A\subseteq\mathbb{Z}$ , denoted $r(A)$ , is defined as the smallest integer $r\geq 0$ such that there is a set $X\subseteq\mathbb{Z}$ of size $r$ satisfying $A\subseteq X+X$ .

This notion has been considered before in the additive combinatorics literature, see, e.g., [32, 22].44 4 In [32, 22], no explicit name is given for the measure in Definition 1.3. Our name rank is inspired both from the connection to [36], and since, coincidentally, the name $[2]$ -sumset rank has already been used in some previous work [23]. Observe that the rank of $A$ ranges from $\lceil\sqrt{|A|}\rceil$ to $|A|+1$ . Sets with low rank are considered structured; for instance intervals or arithmetic progressions have rank close to $\sqrt{|A|}$ . At the other extreme, random-like sets have rank close to $|A|$ . We show that for sets with rank up to $|A|^{1-\epsilon}$ , 3SUM can be solved in subquadratic time:

#### 1.4Informal Theorem 4.1.

Let $\epsilon>0$ . Any 3SUM instance $(A,B,C)$ where one of the sets has rank at most $O(n^{1-\epsilon})$ can be solved in time $O(n^{2-\epsilon^{\prime}})$ for some $\epsilon^{\prime}>0$ .

Interestingly, Theorem 1.4 generalizes and unifies all previously known special cases of 3SUM that are known to be in truly subquadratic time:

- • Small-Universe 3SUM: When $A,B,C\subseteq[u]$ , 3SUM can be solved in time $\widetilde{O}(u)$ by the Fast Fourier Transform. This is truly subquadratic when $u\leq n^{2-\epsilon}$ . In this case, all three sets have rank $O(\sqrt{u})\leq n^{1-\epsilon/2}$ (witnessed by $X=\{0,1,\ldots,\lceil\sqrt{u}\rceil-1\}\cup\{\lceil\sqrt{u}\rceil,2\lceil\sqrt{u}\rceil,\ldots,\lceil\sqrt{u}\rceil^{2}\}$ ).

- • Small-Doubling 3SUM: As a vast generalization to Small-Universe 3SUM, Abboud, Bringmann, and Fischer [1] and Jin and Xu [40] considered 3SUM on inputs with $|A+A|\leq K|A|$ , and gave truly subquadratic time algorithm provided $K\leq n^{\delta}$ where $\delta>0$ is sufficiently small.55 5 A related problem, though significantly simpler, is to solve 3SUM when $|A+B|$ or $|A-B|$ is small; see [14, 35]. For example, [40]’s algorithm for this case runs in $\widetilde{O}(Kn^{1.5})$ time, which is truly subquadratic provided $K\leq n^{0.5-\epsilon}$ . As an improvement to their algorithms, our Theorem 1.4 implies a truly subquadratic 3SUM algorithm whenever $K\leq n^{1-\epsilon}$ . This implication follows from the following simple fact: if $|A+A|\leq|A|^{2-\delta}$ , then there exists a set $X$ of size $|X|\leq\widetilde{O}(|A|^{1-\delta/2})$ such that $A\subseteq X+X$ . Such $X$ exists by a simple probabilistic argument: Pick random subsets $Y\subseteq-A$ and $Z\subseteq A+A$ with sizes $|Y|,|Z|=\Theta(|A|^{1-\delta/2}\sqrt{\log|A|})$ and let $X=Y\cup Z$ . Since each $a\in A$ is represented as $a=y+z$ by at least $|A|$ distinct pairs $(y,z)\in(-A)\times(A+A)$ , with high probability at least one pair $(y,z)$ survives in $Y\cup Z$ for every $a\in A$ .

- • Clustered 3SUM. Chan and Lewenstein [25] studied clustered 3SUM, where a set is clustered if it can be covered by $n^{1-\delta}$ intervals of length $n$ for some $\delta>0$ . They showed a truly subquadratic-time algorithm for this case. It is simple to show that if $A$ is clustered, then a low-rank decomposition of $A$ can be found efficiently: Let $S$ be the set of the smallest numbers in each of the intervals. Then notice that $A\subseteq X+X$ where $X=(S+\{0,1,\ldots,n^{\delta/2}\})\cup\{n^{\delta/2},2n^{\delta/2},\ldots,n\}$ , which has size $O(n^{1-\delta/2})$ .66 6 Chan and Lewenstein also studied a generalization of clustered 3SUM where the inputs are from $\mathbb{Z}^{d}$ for constant $d$ . 3SUM with inputs from $\mathbb{Z}^{d}$ is essentially the same as 3SUM with integer inputs: Given a 3SUM instance with inputs from $\mathbb{Z}^{d}$ , we can map each input vector to an integer by viewing the vector as the $d$ -digit representation of the integer in some large enough base. In the clustered case, when $A\subseteq S+H$ , where $|S|\leq n^{1-\delta}$ and $H$ is a hypercube of volume at most $n$ , their algorithm also runs in truly subquadratic time. Similar as the integer case, we can write $H$ as the sum of $Y+Z$ where $Y$ has size $O(n^{\delta})$ and $Z$ has $O(n^{1-\delta})$ (this is possible because $H$ is a hypercube). Hence, letting $X=(S+Y)\cup Z$ guarantees that $A\subseteq X+X$ and $|X|\leq O(n^{1-\delta/2})$ .

### 1.4 Universe Reduction for Min-Plus Convolution

Having stated our two main technical innovations, let us finally turn to our results involving Min-Plus Convolution. We start with our universe reduction. Here, by universe $[u]$ we refer to the range of the entries in the sequences $A$ and $B$ . Recall that the Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis postulates that the min-plus convolution $A*B$ of two given sequences $A,B$ cannot be computed in subquadratic time. In this hypothesis, as is common in fine-grained complexity, the assumption is that the universe is polynomially bounded, $u=n^{O(1)}$ . A stronger hypothesis, the Strong Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis, postulates that subquadratic time is impossible even for sequences over the universe $[n]$ :

#### 1.5Strong Min-Plus Convolution.

Min-Plus Convolution over the universe $[n]$ cannot be solved in time $O(n^{2-\epsilon})$ for any constant $\epsilon>0$ .

For even smaller universes, however, there are faster algebraic algorithms. Specifically, the Min-Plus Convolution problem can be reduced to computing the sumset of two integer sets in $\{0,\dots,nu\}$ , leading to an alternative $\widetilde{O}(nu)$ -time algorithm using the FFT. This algorithm differs substantially from the naive brute-force algorithm, suggesting that in this small-universe regime ( $u\ll n$ ) the Min-Plus Convolution problem might behave quite differently than in the large-universe regime ( $u\gg n$ ). Thus, a natural question is whether this $\widetilde{O}(nu)$ could be improved, perhaps by some more elaborate algebraic technique? Investigating this question is also highly relevant for the Min-Plus Convolution problem as a source of hardness, as many lower bounds under the Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis could be strengthened if we could assume hardness for small universes. We successfully resolve this question, proving that time $\widetilde{O}(nu)$ is best-possible across all ranges of $u\leq n$ :

#### 1.6Small-Universe Reduction.

Let $\gamma\in[0,1]$ . Min-Plus Convolution for length- $n$ input sequences over a universe of size $u=n^{\gamma}$ cannot be solved in time $O(n^{1+\gamma-\epsilon})$ (for any constant $\epsilon>0$ ), unless the Strong Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis fails.

Even more ambitiously, can one also show a reduction from the large-universe regime? Is there a universe reduction from, say, $u=n^{10}$ to $u=n$ ? We almost answer this question in the affirmative. Unfortunately, in analogy with [36], there remains one key step in our proof for which the state-of-the-art additive combinatorics tools are not strong enough yet. For this reason, Fischer encapsulated the missing structural statement as the following plausible hypothesis. Let us call a function $h:X\to\mathbb{Z}$ sum-order-preserving if, for every $x_{1},x_{2},y_{1},y_{2}\in X$ , $x_{1}+x_{2}<y_{1}+y_{2}$ implies $h(x_{1})+h(x_{2})<h(y_{1})+h(y_{2})$ .

#### 1.7[36].

There is a constant $c$ such that the following holds. For every set of integers $X$ with doubling $|X+X|\leq K|X|$ , there is a subset $Y\subseteq X$ of size $|Y|\geq|X|/K^{c}$ and a sum-order-preserving function $h:Y\rightarrow\{0,1,\ldots,|X|\}$ . Moreover, given $X$ , one can compute $Y$ and $h$ in time $|X|^{1+o(1)}K^{O(1)}$ .

Intuitively, Hypothesis 1.7 speculates that every low-doubling integer set can be compressed to an interval in such a way that the order of pairwise sums is preserved. This statement is closely related to the Polynomial Freiman–Ruzsa (PFR) Conjecture for integers, which, if true, would almost resolve Hypothesis 1.7. Currently, the state-of-the-art bounds [48] together with the work of [6] imply that one can take $\exp((\log K)^{1+o(1)})$ instead of $K^{c}$ in Hypothesis 1.7. We therefore hope that Hypothesis 1.7 will eventually be resolved alongside the PFR Conjecture. We refer to [36] for a more detailed discussion of this hypothesis and its plausibility.

Under Hypothesis 1.7 we do obtain the full universe reduction:

#### 1.8Large-Universe Reduction.

Under Hypothesis 1.7, the Strong Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis and the Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis are equivalent.

In summary, under Hypothesis 1.7, Theorems 1.6 and 1.8 fully characterize the complexity of Min-Plus Convolution as $\min\{n^{2},nu\}^{1\pm o(1)}$ for all universe sizes $u=n^{\Theta(1)}$ . If this algorithm can be improved in any regime, then the Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis fails.

### 1.5 Application to Intermediate Convolution Problems

Fischer [36] also showed a list of APSP-based tight conditional lower bounds for “intermediate” problems, a well-studied class of matrix problems whose running times are about $n^{2.5}$ when $\omega=2$ . Likewise, our techniques also allow us to show matching conditional lower bounds for a range of intermediate sequence problems, whose best known running times are $\widetilde{O}(n^{1.5})$ .

#### Min-Max Convolution.

In the Min-Max Convolution problem, we are given sequences $A,B$ of length $n$ , and need to compute a sequence $C$ where $C[k]=\min_{i+j=k}\max\{A[i],B[j]\}$ . Bringmann, Künnemann and Węgrzycki [17] showed that this problem is equivalent to approximate Min-Plus Convolution. An $\widetilde{O}(n^{1.5})$ time algorithm for computing Min-Max Convolution was known as early as 1989 [44]. However, no further improvements were known since then, and there is also no strong evidence why this running time might be optimal. We show a tight conditional lower bound for Min-Max Convolution.

#### 1.9Min-Max Convolution.

Min-Max Convolution cannot be solved in time $O(n^{3/2-\epsilon})$ (for any constant $\epsilon>0$ ), unless the Strong Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis fails.

#### Min-Equality Convolution.

In the Min-Equality Convolution problem, we are given sequences $A,B$ of length $n$ , and need to compute a sequence $C$ where

$$ C[k]=\min_{\begin{subarray}{c}i+j=k\\
A[i]=B[j]\end{subarray}}A[i]. $$

Previously, it was studied by Chan, Vassilevska Williams and Xu [26], who showed that Min-Equality Convolution requires $n^{12/11-o(1)}$ time, under the Strong Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis (they also showed an $n^{7/6-o(1)}$ lower bound based on the Strong APSP Hypothesis and an $n^{5/4-o(1)}$ lower bound based on the unweighted directed APSP Hypothesis, but neither matches the $\widetilde{O}(n^{1.5})$ upper bound). In our work, we significantly improve their result, by showing a tight lower bound based on the Strong Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis.

#### 1.10Min-Equality Convolution.

Min-Equality Convolution cannot be solved in time $O(n^{3/2-\epsilon})$ (for any constant $\epsilon>0$ ), unless the Strong Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis fails.

#### Bounded Monotone Min-Plus Convolution.

Bounded Monotone Min-Plus Convolution is a version of Min-Plus Convolution with structured inputs. A length- $n$ sequence is called bounded monotone if all entries are from $[O(n)]$ , and the sequence is monotonically nondecreasing. Chan and Lewenstein [25] were the first to study Bounded Monotone Min-Plus Convolution: they showed that when both input sequences are bounded monotone, Min-Plus Convolution can be computed in $O(n^{1.859})$ time. This running time has been improved to $\widetilde{O}(n^{1.5})$ by Chi, Duan, Xie and Zhang [30], and Bringmann, Dürr and Polak [13] generalized their algorithm to the case where only one of the sequences needs to be bounded monotone. Bounded-Monotone Min-Plus Convolution has found a variety of applications, including Jumbled Indexing [25] and several variants of knapsack [12, 13, 28]. We show that [13]’s algorithm is conditionally optimal:

#### 1.11Bounded Monotone Min-Plus Convolution.

Min-Plus Convolution between an arbitrary sequence and a monotone sequence bounded by $[n]$ cannot be solved in time $O(n^{3/2-\epsilon})$ (for any constant $\epsilon>0$ ), unless the Strong Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis fails.

#### Min-Witness Convolution.

Given two length- $n$ Boolean sequences $A,B$ , their Min-Witness Convolution $C$ is defined such as $C[k]$ equals the minimum index $i$ where $A[i]$ and $B[k-i]$ are both true. This problem has been listed in papers studying fine-grained complexity of intermediate problems [47, 26] as a natural target for proving conditional lower bound for, but there has been no nontrivial lower bound so far for this problem. We prove the first super-linear (albeit non-tight) conditional lower bound for Min-Witness Convolution:

#### 1.12Min-Witness Convolution.

Min-Witness Convolution cannot be solved in time $O(n^{4/3-\epsilon})$ (for any constant $\epsilon>0$ ), unless the Strong Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis fails.

A careful reader might have noticed that our lower bounds for intermediate sequence problems are based on the Strong Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis, while Fischer [36]’s lower bounds for intermediate matrix problems are based on the APSP Hypothesis itself rather than its strong variant. Without relying on Hypothesis 1.7, Fischer first reduced APSP to a version of Min-Plus Product where the universe has low-doubling (rather than simply an interval $[u]$ ), and then obtained APSP-based lower bounds for intermediate matrix problems from this first step. We also manage to prove an analogous version of the first step in Min-Plus Convolution (Lemma 5.3); unfortunately, it seems hard to obtain tight reductions for intermediate sequence problems from it. Intuitively, one reason why it is harder to design reductions to intermediate sequence problems is the following: In Fischer’s universe reduction for APSP, both the inner dimension and the universe of the Min-Plus Product are reduced, which make it easier to further reduce to intermediate matrix problems. In contrast, for sequence problems, there is no analogue of an “inner dimension”, so there is less room to work with in downstream reductions.

### 1.6 Proof Ideas

In this section we give a quick high-level overview for the results we have not sketched before.

#### 1.6.1 Low-Rank 3SUM in Subquadratic Time

We start with the ideas behind our subquadratic-time algorithm for low-rank 3SUM. Let $(A,B,C)$ denote a given 3SUM instance, and assume that $C\subseteq X+X$ for some small set, $|X|\leq n^{1-\epsilon}$ . At the heart of our algorithm lies a curious win-win paradigm: Either we can solve the instance by a clever brute-force algorithm, or we can amplify structure.

Specifically, to find a 3SUM solution $a+b=c$ we could try to enumerate all solutions

$$ a+b=x_{1}+x_{2},\qquad\text{for $a\in A,b\in B,x_{1},x_{2}\in X$.} $$

For each such solution we can test if $a+b=x_{1}+x_{2}$ is actually an element in $C$ ; only then have we found a solution. This might seem like overkill—after all we are listing many more solutions than necessary. But the crucial advantage is that solutions to this equation can be listed very efficiently. Indeed, rewriting each solution as

$$ a-x_{1}=x_{2}-b, $$

a natural meet-in-the-middle algorithm is to preprocess the sets $A-X$ and $X-B$ in time $O(|A|\,|X|+|B|\,|X|)=O(n^{2-\epsilon})$ . Afterwards, we can list all solutions in time $O(N)$ , where $N$ denotes the number of solutions. If $N\leq n^{2-\delta}$ , say, then this algorithm runs in subquadratic time. But of course, $N$ might be much larger, possibly up to $|X|^{2}n=n^{3-2\epsilon}$ , and in that case the meet-in-the-middle strategy is doomed.

Our key insight is that, in this situation, the sets $A$ and $B$ admit amplified structure. Concretely, focus on $B$ . For simplicity, assume that all elements $b\in B$ participate in roughly the same number of solutions to Equation 1, i.e., in about $N/|B|$ solutions. Then, in other words, each $b\in B$ is an $N/|B|\geq n^{1-\delta}$ -popular sum in the set $X+X-A$ . Note that we started from the structural information that $C\subseteq X+X$ , but ended up with the information that $B$ is covered by the $n^{1-\delta}$ -popular sums in $X+X-A$ . It turns out that this argument can be iterated. By arguing as above, but exchanging the roles of $B$ and $C$ , we can either solve the instance, or further derive that $C$ is covered by the $n^{2-2\delta}$ -popular sums in $X+X-A+A$ . And iterating this argument $k$ times, we eventually infer that $C$ is covered by the $n^{2k-2k\delta}$ -popular sums in $X+X-kA+kA$ .

At this point, $C$ witnesses an $n^{2k-2k\delta}$ -popular sum in $X+X-kA+kA$ . This is where our structure theorem (Theorem 1.2) comes into play. When carefully applied, it implies that there is some low-doubling set $H$ of size at about $|X|^{2}n^{2k\delta}\leq n^{2-2\epsilon+2k\delta}$ that covers a large fraction of $A$ . Here, intuitively think of $\delta$ as an extremely small constant, so that the $2k\delta$ term effectively becomes $0$ . That is, intuitively, we have showed that $A$ is covered by a low-doubling set of size $|X|^{2}$ . All in all, it is quite intriguing how the structure amplifies: We start from a weakly structured set $C$ , then infer some more structure for $B$ , then again for $C$ , and so on. And eventually, we conclude that $A$ admits a small low-doubling container. Besides, it is interesting that for a 3SUM algorithm the relevant structure lies in the number of $k$ -sums.

Of course, we are not completely done. What remains is a 3SUM instance $(A,B,C)$ equipped with a container set $H\supseteq A$ of size $|H|\leq n^{2-\epsilon}$ and with arbitrarily low doubling. But this instance can be dealt with following ideas that have already appeared in earlier work (notably, [40]), and for this reason we defer further details to Section 4.

#### 1.6.2 Universe Reduction for Min-Plus Convolution

Finally, we give a brief glimpse into our new universe reduction. Only at this point will it become clear why the rank of a set is a reasonable notion in our context.

For concreteness, focus on the universe reduction from $[n]$ to $[\sqrt{n}]$ . That is, we argue that if Min-Plus Convolution over the universe $[\sqrt{n}]$ is in time $O(n^{3/2-\epsilon})$ , then Min-Plus Convolution over the universe $[n]$ is in time $O(n^{2-\epsilon^{\prime}})$ (contradicting the Strong Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis). Let $A,B$ denote the given length- $n$ sequences over the universe $[n]$ . We rewrite the sequences into their base- $\sqrt{n}$ representation as

$$ \displaystyle A \displaystyle=A_{1}\cdot q+A_{0}, \displaystyle B \displaystyle=B_{1}\cdot q+B_{0}, $$

where the four sequences $A_{0},B_{0},A_{1},B_{1}$ are each over the universe $[\sqrt{n}]$ . Let us call an index $i$ a witness of $k$ if $(A*B)[k]=A[i]+B[k-i]$ , and a pseudo-witness if $(A_{1}*B_{1})[k]=A_{1}[i]+B_{1}[k-i]$ . Equivalently, the pseudo-witnesses are those indices that would become indices when rounding $A,B$ to multiples of $\sqrt{n}$ . By standard approaches, we can assume $A_{0}$ and $B_{0}$ have entries less than $\sqrt{n}/2$ , so that a witness must be a pseudo-witness.

We will now execute the structure-versus-randomness paradigm that we sketched in the beginning. The notion of pseudo-randomness turns out to concern the number of pseudo-witnesses: in a pseudo-random instance, all indices $k$ have few pseudo-witnesses, say at most $n^{1/2+\epsilon/2}$ . This is indeed a good case for our reduction, as we can afford to list all pseudo-witnesses. Notably, this list also contains the true witnesses. To obtain the list of pseudo-witnesses, we apply a simple sampling trick (Lemma 2.14), reducing the listing problem to $\widetilde{O}(n^{1/2+\epsilon/2})$ plain min-plus convolutions of restrictions of $A_{1}$ and $B_{1}$ . These are sequences over the universe $[\sqrt{n}]$ , and can thus be convolved in time $O(n^{3/2-\epsilon})$ by our initial assumption. The total time is $O(n^{2-\epsilon/2})$ .

Of course, we first need to transform the initial instance $(A,B)$ into a pseudo-random one, and this is where the rank becomes relevant. To simplify in this overview, suppose that all indices $k$ have many (i.e., more than $n^{1/2+\epsilon/2}$ ) pseudo-witnesses.77 7 In fact, this idealized situation is impossible. For instance, $k=0$ always has exactly one (pseudo-)witness, namely $i=0$ . But this is a technicality that shall not concern us in this overview. In this case, so we claim, the whole instance has low rank and can directly be solved in subquadratic time. To see this, we first apply the standard reduction from Min-Plus Convolution to 3SUM: We approximate $C\approx A*B$ (by some standard trick, with coordinate-wise constant additive error), then replace the sequences $A,B,C$ by their indexed sets

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{A} \displaystyle=\{(i,A[i]):0\leq i\leq n\}, \displaystyle\mathcal{B} \displaystyle=\{(j,B[j]):0\leq j\leq n\}, \displaystyle\mathcal{C} \displaystyle=\{(k,C[k]):0\leq k\leq 2n\}, $$

and solve the remaining 3SUM instance $(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C})$ . These are 2-dimensional sets that can be flattened to plain integers via the usual embedding. We argue that $\mathcal{C}$ has low rank, $r(\mathcal{C})\leq\tilde{O}(n^{1-\epsilon/4})$ . This can be shown in two steps:

- • First, consider the set

$$ \mathcal{C}_{1}=\{(k,(A_{1}*B_{1})[k]\cdot\sqrt{n}):0\leq k\leq 2n\}. $$

Assuming that each $k$ has many pseudo-witnesses, we can sample a set of $\tilde{O}(n^{3/4-\epsilon/4})$ indices $X\subseteq[0,n]$ . With good probability, for each $k$ we include some witness $i\in X$ and simultaneously also $k-i\in X$ . In this case, the set

$$ \mathcal{X}_{1}=\{(i,A_{1}[i]\cdot\sqrt{n}):i\in X\}\cup\{(j,B_{1}[j]\cdot\sqrt{n}):j\in X\} $$

satisfies $\mathcal{C}_{1}\subseteq\mathcal{X}_{1}+\mathcal{X}_{1}$ , witnessing that $r(\mathcal{C}_{1})\leq|\mathcal{X}_{1}|\leq O(n^{3/4-\epsilon/4})$ .

- • Second, note that $\mathcal{C}_{1}$ is an indexed set that approximates $\mathcal{C}$ well. Indeed, for any $c\in\mathcal{C}$ , there exists $c_{1}\in\mathcal{C}_{1}$ such that $c-c_{1}\in\mathcal{I}$ , where $\mathcal{I}=\{(0,0),\dots,(0,\sqrt{n})\}$ . Hence, we can expand $\mathcal{X}_{1}$ to $\mathcal{X}$ so that $\mathcal{X}_{1}+\mathcal{X}_{1}+\mathcal{I}\subseteq\mathcal{X}+\mathcal{X}$ , which will then imply $\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathcal{X}+\mathcal{X}$ . To achieve this, we set

$$ \mathcal{X}=\mathcal{X}_{1}\cup\left\{(0,0),(0,1),\ldots,(0,n^{1/4})\right\}\cup\left\{(0,n^{1/4}),(0,2\cdot n^{1/4}),\ldots,(0,\sqrt{n})\right\}. $$

Finally, $r(\mathcal{C})\leq|\mathcal{X}|\leq O(n^{1-\epsilon/4})$ .

In summary, our low-rank 3SUM algorithm (Theorem 4.1) can solve the 3SUM instance $(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C})$ in subquadratic time $O(n^{2-\epsilon^{\prime}})$ .

## 2 Preliminaries

We use $[n]$ to denote $\{1,2,\dots,n\}$ for any integer $n\geq 0$ .

### 2.1 Additive Combinatorics

For two sets $A,B\subseteq\mathbb{Z}$ , define their sumset $A+B=\{a+b:a\in A,b\in B\}$ and difference set $A-B=\{a-b:a\in A,b\in B\}$ . Let $-A=\{-a:a\in A\}$ . The $k$ -fold sumset $kA$ is recursively defined by $kA=(k-1)A+A$ with $1A=A$ . Denote $r_{A+B}(z)=|\{(x,y)\in A\times B:x+y=z\}|$ . We often conveniently refer to $r_{A+B}(z)$ as the multiplicity of $z$ in the sumset $A+B$ . Similarly, the multiplicity of $z$ in the $k$ -fold sumset $kA$ means $|\{(x_{1},\dots,x_{k})\in A^{k}:x_{1}+\dots+x_{k}=z\}|$ .

#### 2.1Plünnecke–Ruzsa Inequality.

For two sets $A,B$ , if $|A+B|\leq K|A|$ , then for any integers $n,m\geq 0$ , $|mB-nB|\leq K^{m+n}|A|$ .

#### 2.2Sparse Convolution, [14].

There is a deterministic algorithm that, given $A,B\subseteq[-u,u]$ , computes the sumset $A+B$ along with the multiplicities $r_{A+B}$ in time $|A+B|\cdot(\log u)^{O(1)}$ .

The additive energy between two sets $A,B\subseteq\mathbb{Z}$ is

$$ E(A,B)=\lvert\{(a_{1},a_{2},b_{1},b_{2})\in A^{2}\times B^{2}:a_{1}+b_{1}=a_{2}+b_{2}\}\rvert=\sum_{z}r_{A+B}(z)^{2}. $$

The additive energy of a set $A\subseteq\mathbb{Z}$ is $E(A)=E(A,A)$ . We also define the following standard higher-order analogue of the additive energy, for any integer $k\geq 1$ :

$$ T_{k}(A)=\lvert\{(a_{1},\dots,a_{k},b_{1},\dots,b_{k})\in A^{2k}:a_{1}+\dots+a_{k}=b_{1}+\dots+b_{k}\}\rvert. $$

The Balog–Szemerédi–Gowers (BSG) Theorem was originally proved in [8, 38]. We use the following algorithmic version of the BSG theorem appearing in [1, Theorem 3.3] (which is an adaptation of [25]).

#### 2.3BSG Theorem.

If set $A$ has additive energy $E(A)\geq|A|^{3}/K$ , then there exists a subset $A^{\prime}\subseteq A$ such that

- • $|A^{\prime}|\geq\Omega(K^{-2}|A|)$ , and

- • $|A^{\prime}+A^{\prime}|\leq O(K^{24}|A|)$ .

Moreover, given $A$ and $K$ , we can compute $A^{\prime}$ in time $\widetilde{O}(K^{12}|A|)$ by a randomized algorithm.

The Asymmetric BSG Theorem was proved in the textbook by Tao and Vu [52, Section 2.6]. We need an algorithmic version of this theorem stated below, which we prove in Section 7.

#### 2.4Asymmetric BSG Theorem.

Let $\epsilon>0$ and $0<\alpha\leq 1$ . Let $A,B\subseteq\mathbb{Z}$ be sets with energy $E(A,B)\geq\alpha|A|^{2}|B|$ . Then there are sets $H,\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb{Z}$ and some $K\leq O_{\epsilon}(\alpha^{-O_{\epsilon}(1)}(1+|B|/|A|)^{\epsilon})$ such that:

- • $|H+H|\leq K|H|$ ,

- • $|H|\,|\Lambda|\leq K|B|$ ,

- • $|A\cap H|\geq|A|/K$ and $|B\cap(H+\Lambda)|\geq|B|/K$ .

Moreover, there is a randomized algorithm to compute $H,\Lambda$ in time $\widetilde{O}((|A|+|B|)K)$ .

Related to these tools, we will also need to compute approximations of sumset multiplicities.

#### 2.5Approximating Sumset Multiplicities.

There is a randomized algorithm that, given sets $A,B,C$ and $\epsilon>0$ , computes approximations $\tilde{r}(x)$ , for all $x\in C$ , with additive error

$$ |r_{A+B}(x)-\tilde{r}(x)|\leq\epsilon|A|. $$

The algorithm runs in time $\widetilde{O}(|A|+|B|/\epsilon+|C|)$ .

A proof of Lemma 2.5 can be found in [33, Footnote 6]. See [33, Corollary 3.1] for a derandomization of this algorithm.

### 2.2 Problem Definitions

As is common in fine-grained complexity, hardness hypotheses and reductions implicitly allow Monte-Carlo randomization (though there has been some interest in derandomizing 3SUM-related reductions [24, 34]).

#### 2.63SUM.

Given three sets of integers $A,B,C$ , determine whether there exists $a\in A,b\in B,c\in C$ such that $a+b=c$ . In its All-Integer version we need to determine for every number in the input, whether it participates in a solution $a+b=c$ .

We use $\ThreeSUM(n)$ to denote the running time of 3SUM instances with size- $n$ inputs. We also use $\ThreeSUM(n\mid r\leq R)$ to denote the running time of 3SUM instances where the rank (Definition 1.3) of one of the sets is at most $R$ , and such a rank decomposition is given. A subinstance of a 3SUM instance with input $(A,B,C)$ is another 3SUM instance with input $(A^{\prime},B^{\prime},C^{\prime})$ where $A^{\prime}\subseteq A,B^{\prime}\subseteq B,C^{\prime}\subseteq C$ .

#### 2.7Min-Plus Convolution.

Given two sequences $A,B\in\mathbb{Z}^{[0,n]}$ , compute a sequence $C=A*B\in\mathbb{Z}^{[0,2n]}$ , where $C[k]=\min_{i+j=k}\{A[i]+B[j]\}$ .

We use $\MinPlusConv(n)$ to denote the running time of Min-Plus Convolution instances with size- $n$ inputs. We also use $\MinPlusConv(n\mid u\leq U)$ to denote the running time of Min-Plus Convolution instances where the entries are from $[U]$ .

#### 2.8Min-Plus Convolution Listing.

Given two sequences $A,B\in\mathbb{Z}^{[0,n]}$ , and an integer threshold $t$ , list $t$ witnesses $(i,j)$ where $A[i]+B[j]=(A*B)[k]$ for every $k$ . If there are fewer than $t$ witnesses for certain indices $k$ , list all the witnesses for these indices.

Similar as before, we use $\MinPlusConvListing(n,t)$ and $\MinPlusConvListing(n,t\mid u\leq U)$ to denote the running times. A subinstance of Min-Plus Convolution (and all sequence problems considered in this paper) can be obtained by setting some entries to $\perp$ , a value that cannot be involved in any solution.

#### 2.9Bounded-Monotone Min-Plus Convolution.

Given two sequences $A,B\in\mathbb{Z}^{[0,n]}$ where $B$ is monotonically nondecreasing and has entries in $[O(n)]$ , compute $A*B$ .

#### 2.10Min-Max Convolution.

Given two sequences $A,B\in\mathbb{Z}^{[0,n]}$ , compute a sequence $C=\MinMax(A,B)\in\mathbb{Z}^{[0,2n]}$ , where $C[k]=\min_{i+j=k}\max\{A[i],B[j]\}$ .

#### 2.11Min-Equality Convolution.

Given two sequences $A,B\in\mathbb{Z}^{[0,n]}$ , compute a sequence $C=\MinEqual(A,B)\in\mathbb{Z}^{[0,2n]}$ , where $C[k]=\min_{i+j=k,A[i]=B[j]}A[i]$ .

#### 2.12Min-Witness Convolution.

Given two Boolean sequences $A,B\in\{0,1\}^{[0,n]}$ , compute a sequence $C=\MinWitness(A,B)\in(\mathbb{Z}\cup\{\bot\})^{[0,2n]}$ , where $C[k]=\min\{i\in[0,n]:k-i\in[0,n]\wedge A[i]=B[k-i]=1\}$ (if no such $i$ exists, define $C[k]=\bot$ ).

We now define the index set of a sequence. We will frequently use this notion to convert Min-Plus Convolution instances to 3SUM instances.

#### 2.13Index set $\mathcal{I}(\cdot)$ .

For a sequence $A\in\mathbb{Z}^{[0,n]}$ indexed by integers in $[0,n]$ , the index set of $A$ is $\mathcal{I}(A)=\{(i,A[i]):i\in[0,n]\}$ .

More generally, for a sequence $A\in(\mathbb{Z}\cup\{\bot\})^{[0,n]}$ , the index set of $A$ is $\mathcal{I}(A)=\{(i,A[i]):i\in[0,n],A[i]\neq\bot\}$ .

### 2.3 Reduction from Listing to Non-Listing Problems

For most problems considered in this paper, one can use an algorithm for the non-listing version of a problem to list witnesses, via a standard approach based on sampling and parallel binary search (e.g., [4, 49]). This is summarized in the following lemma.

#### 2.14Listing Witnesses for Convolution Problems.

Any Min-Plus Convolution Listing instance $(A,B)$ with threshold $t$ can be reduced to $t(\log n)^{O(1)}$ Min-Plus Convolution (non-Listing) subinstances. The reduction runs in time $\widetilde{O}(nt)$ . In particular,

$$ \MinPlusConvListing(n,t\mid u)\leq\widetilde{O}(t\cdot\MinPlusConv(n\mid u)). $$

Moreover, for any $t_{1},t_{2}\geq 1$ ,

$$ \MinPlusConvListing(n,t_{1}t_{2}\mid u)\leq\widetilde{O}(t_{1}\cdot\MinPlusConvListing(n,t_{2}\mid u)). $$

The same statements also hold with “Min-Plus” replaced by “Min-Max” and “Min-Equality”.

We omit the proof of Lemma 2.14 here since it is standard. We refer readers to [36, Section 5.1] for a proof in the analogous setting of Min-Plus Matrix Product, which can be adapted to Min-Plus Convolution in a straightforward manner. The same proof strategy also applies to Min-Max Convolution and Min-Equality Convolution.88 8 En route we rely on a sampling-based approach, which requires setting some input values to $\perp$ , so that they cannot be used in any solution (see [36, Section 5.1]). In the problems we consider, $\perp$ can be replaced with actual numbers without heavily affecting the problem sizes. In Min-Plus Convolution with universe $[u]$ , we can simply set $\perp$ to $2u+1$ , so they can never participate in a solution with value less than or equal to $2u$ , while all the solutions obtained from non- $\perp$ values have value at most $2u$ . Similarly, in Min-Max Convolution with universe $[u]$ , we can simply set $\perp$ to $u+1$ . In Min-Equality Convolution, we can set $\perp$ in $A$ and in $B$ to be two different special values that do not occur in the non- $\perp$ values of $A,B$ .

The same sampling strategy together with FFT yields the following more well-known lemma for listing witnesses of Boolean Convolution:

#### 2.15.

Given two sequences $A,B\in\{0,1\}^{[0,n]}$ and a threshold $t\geq 1$ , one can compute their Boolean Convolution $C\in\{0,1\}^{[0,2n]}$ defined as $C[k]=\bigvee_{i+j=k}(A[i]\land B[j])$ , and additionally, for each $k$ , list up to $t$ witnesses $i$ such that $A[i]=B[k-i]=1$ , in $\widetilde{O}(tn)$ time.

## 3 Popular $k$ -Sum Structure

The goal of this section is to prove Theorem 1.2. We start with some basic definitions and facts.

#### 3.1Popular $k$ -Sums.

Let $A_{1},\dots,A_{k}\subseteq\mathbb{Z}$ , and $p>0$ . The set $\Pop(A_{1},\dots,A_{k};p)$ consists of all integers $x$ that can be expressed in at least $p$ distinct ways as

$$ x=a_{1}+\dots+a_{k} $$

for $(a_{1},\dots,a_{k})\in A_{1}\times\dots\times A_{k}$ ; we call these the $p$ -popular $k$ -sums. When $A=A_{1}=\dots=A_{k}$ , we simply write $\Pop^{k}(A;p)$ .

The following simple observation will be useful later.

#### 3.2.

If $\Pop(A_{1},\dots,A_{k};p)\neq\emptyset$ then $\Pop(A_{2},\dots,A_{k};p/|A_{1}|)\neq\emptyset$ .

See 1.2

The following lemma is based on simple random sampling. Its version for $k=2$ has been considered before (e.g., [40]).

#### 3.3Approximating Popular Sums.

There is a randomized algorithm that, given sets $A_{1},\dots,A_{k}\subseteq\mathbb{Z}$ and an integer threshold $p\geq 1$ , computes a set $P$ such that

$$ \Pop(A_{1},\dots,A_{k};2p)\subseteq P\subseteq\Pop(A_{1},\dots,A_{k};p) $$

in randomized time

$$ \widetilde{O}\left\lparen\frac{|A_{1}|\,\dots\,|A_{k}|}{p}\right\rparen. $$

Denote $A=A_{1}\times\dots\times A_{k}$ . For a large constant $C$ , we uniformly independently sample $m=\lceil\frac{C|A|\log|A|}{p}\rceil$ $k$ -tuples $t_{1},t_{2},\dots,t_{m}\in A$ . Let $s_{i}$ denote the sum of the $k$ components in the tuple $t_{i}$ . Let $\tilde{f}_{x}$ denote the number of times the integer $x$ occurs in the list of sums $(s_{1},\dots,s_{m})$ . Let $P$ be the set of all integers $x$ with $\tilde{f}_{x}\geq 1.5p\cdot\frac{m}{|A|}$ . We compute and return $P$ in $\widetilde{O}(m)=\widetilde{O}(\frac{|A_{1}|\,\dots\,|A_{k}|}{p})$ time.

We now show that $P$ satisfies the claimed property with high probability. For every integer $x$ , if $x$ can be expressed in $f_{x}$ ways as $x=a_{1}+\dots+a_{k}$ for $(a_{1},\dots,a_{k})\in A$ , then $\Pr[s_{i}=x]=f_{x}/|A|$ for every $1\leq i\leq m$ . Hence, if $f_{x}\geq 2p$ , then by Chernoff bound, $x\notin P$ happens with probability $\Pr[\tilde{f}_{x}<1.5p\cdot\frac{m}{|A|}]\leq\exp(-\frac{pm}{16|A|})\leq|A|^{-C/16}$ . If $f_{x}<p$ , then by Chernoff bound, $x\in P$ happens with probability $\Pr[\tilde{f}_{x}\geq 1.5p\cdot\frac{m}{|A|}]\leq\exp(-\frac{pm}{12|A|})\leq|A|^{-C/12}$ . By a union bound over all $x\in A_{1}+\dots+A_{k}$ , we conclude that $P$ is correct with high probability in $|A|$ . ∎

### 3.1 Qualitative Optimality

Let us briefly comment that Theorem 1.2 is (qualitatively) optimal. For every $c>0$ and every integer $k\geq 2$ , there is a small enough $\epsilon\in(0,1)$ that would violate the theorem statement. More specifically, there is a family of size- $n$ sets $A$ such that $\Pop^{k}(A;p)\neq\emptyset$ for some $p=\Omega(|A|^{k-1-c})$ , and so that any set $H$ with $|A\cap H|\geq n^{1-\epsilon}$ and $|H|\leq n^{1+c+\epsilon}$ would have doubling constant much larger than $n^{\epsilon}$ . The same proof would also show for every $\epsilon\in(0,1)$ and every $k\geq 2$ , there exists $c>0$ that violates the theorem statement. This shows that $k$ in the theorem necessarily depends on $c$ and $\epsilon$ (though the dependence could possibly be improved to linear in $c/\epsilon$ ).

Indeed, take $A=I+R$ where $I$ is an interval (or any other low-doubling set) of size $n^{1-c/(k-1)}$ , and where $R$ is a random set of size $n^{c/(k-1)}$ that is not correlated with $H$ . By taking $R$ from a large enough universe, we can assume that, for every $\ell\leq(c+2)\log n$ , there is no $\ell$ -term additive relation

$$ (i_{1}+r_{1})+\cdots+(i_{\ell}+r_{\ell})=(i_{\ell+1}+r_{\ell+1})+\cdots+(i_{2\ell}+r_{2\ell}), $$

where $r_{1},\ldots,r_{2\ell}$ are distinct, while $i_{1},\ldots,i_{2\ell}$ might not. Then $A$ has size roughly $|I|\,|R|=n$ . Moreover, $\Pop^{k}(A;|A|^{k-1-c})$ is non-empty as each sum $r_{1}+\cdots+r_{k}\in kR$ can be extended in about $|I|^{k-1}=n^{k-1-c}$ ways to a common popular sum in $kI+kR$ . Take $H$ to be any set where $|H|\leq n^{1+c+\epsilon}$ and $|A\cap H|\geq n^{1-\epsilon}$ . By pigeonhole principle, $A\cap H$ must contain $p_{t}=i_{t}+r_{t}$ for $i_{t}\in I,r_{t}\in R$ where the values $r_{t}$ are distinct, for some $t\geq n^{1-\epsilon}/n^{1-c/(k-1)}=n^{c/(k-1)-\epsilon}$ . By our assumption on $R$ , there is no $\ell$ -term additive relation for numbers $P=\{p_{1},\ldots,p_{t}\}$ for every $\ell\leq(c+2)\log n$ .

Now consider the additive energy $E(P,H)$ . For every nontrivial solution, $p_{1}+h_{1}=p_{2}+h_{2}$ for $p_{1},p_{2}\in P$ and $h_{1},h_{2}\in H$ , we consider adding an edge between $h_{1}$ and $h_{2}$ . Note that an $\ell$ -cycle in this graph induces an $\ell$ -term additive relation for numbers $P$ . Hence, the girth of this graph is $>(c+2)\log n$ , which implies that the number of edges is $O(|H|)$ by the graph Moore bound [5]. Hence, $E(P,H)$ is dominated by the trivial solutions, so $E(P,H)=O(|P||H|)$ . By Cauchy–Schwarz inequality,

$$ |P+H|=\sum_{z}[r_{P+H}(z)>0]\geq\frac{(\sum_{z}r_{P+H}(z))^{2}}{\sum_{z}r_{P+H}(z)^{2}}\geq\frac{|P|^{2}|H|^{2}}{O(|P||H|)}\geq\Omega(|P||H|). $$

As $|H+H|\geq|P+H|$ , the doubling constant of $H$ is at least $\Omega(|P|)=\Omega(n^{c/(k-1)})$ , which is greater than $n^{\epsilon}$ when $k\ll\frac{c}{\epsilon}$ .

### 3.2 Existential Proof

It is more convenient to re-express having popular sums in terms of the higher-order energy $T_{k}(A)$ . [50]. The proof relies on the following lemma:

#### 3.4.

For every $\epsilon,c>0$ , there is some $k=k(c,\epsilon)$ such that the following holds. Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{Z}$ be such that $T_{k}(A)\geq\Omega(|A|^{2k-1-c})$ . Then there exists a set $H\subseteq\mathbb{Z}$ and some $K=O_{c,\epsilon}(|A|^{\epsilon})$ such that:

- • $|H|\leq K|A|^{1+c}$ ,

- • $|H+H|\leq K|H|$ ,

- • $|A\cap H|\geq|A|/K$ .

Let us postpone the proof of Lemma 3.4 for the moment, and first see how Theorem 1.2 can be concluded from the lemma.

Let $k=k(\epsilon,c)$ be chosen as in Lemma 3.4. Let $A$ be a set with a $p$ -popular $2k$ -sum $z$ for some $p=\Omega(|A|^{2k-1-c})$ . $$ D^{2}\cdot E(A,P_{D})\geq|A|^{2k-1-c-o(1)}. $$

$$ |A\cap H|\geq\frac{|A|}{K}, $$

### 3.3 Efficient Algorithm

We finally revisit the previous proof to demonstrate that all steps can be implemented efficiently, leading to the following algorithmic theorem:

#### 3.5.

For every $c>0$ and $\epsilon>0$ , there is some $k=k(c,\epsilon)$ such that the following holds. There is a randomized algorithm that, given $A\subseteq\mathbb{Z}$ and some parameter $p=\Omega(|A|^{k-1-c})$ , either certifies that $\Pop^{k}(A;p)=\emptyset$ , or otherwise computes a set $H\subseteq\mathbb{Z}$ such that the following properties hold for some $K\leq O(|A|^{\epsilon})$ :

- • $|H|\leq K|A|^{1+c}$ ,

- • $|H+H|\leq K|H|$ ,

- • $|A\cap H|\geq|A|/K$ .

The algorithm runs in time $\widetilde{O}(|A|^{1+c+\epsilon})$ .

The following lemma is analogous to Lemma 3.4.

#### 3.6.

For every $\epsilon,c>0$ , there is some $k=k(c,\epsilon)$ such that the following holds. There is a randomized algorithm that, given $A\subseteq\mathbb{Z}$ such that $T_{k}(A)\geq\Omega(|A|^{2k-1-c})$ computes a set $H\subseteq\mathbb{Z}$ such that the following properties hold for some $K\leq O(|A|^{\epsilon})$ :

- • $|H|\leq K|A|^{1+c}$ ,

- • $|H+H|\leq K|H|$ ,

- • $|A\cap H|\geq|A|/K$ .

We choose $k=k(c,\epsilon)$ as in Lemma 3.6. Given $A$ , we first apply Lemma 3.3 to compute a set $P$ satisfying (with high probability) that

$$ \Pop^{k}(A;p)\subseteq P\subseteq\Pop^{k}(A;p/2). $$

If $P=\emptyset$ , then we have certified that $\Pop^{k}(A;p)=\emptyset$ . So suppose otherwise that $P$ contains some element $z$ . We are guaranteed that $z$ is a $p/2$ -popular $k$ -sum in $A$ . We call Lemma 3.6 on the set $A^{*}=\pm(A\cup\{z\})$ with parameter $p/2$ . As before, it holds that $T_{k}(A^{*})\geq p/2$ and thus Lemma 3.6 computes a set $H\subseteq\mathbb{Z}$ which is as claimed, except that instead of the third condition we have $|A^{*}\cap H|\geq|A|/K$ . However, as $A^{*}$ is a union of four copies of $A$ , possibly translated and negated, one of the corresponding translations and/or negations of $H$ must satisfy the claim. We test all four and verify each in linear time. The total time is dominated by the calls to Lemmas 3.3 and 3.6, running in time $\tilde{O}(|A|^{k}/p)=\tilde{O}(|A|^{1+c})$ and $O(|A|^{1+c+\epsilon})$ , respectively. ∎

Following the proof of Lemma 3.4, we design a recursive algorithm. If $T_{k}(A)$ is sufficiently large as in the lemma statement, then the algorithm returns $H$ satisfying the claimed properties with high probability. If the bound on $T_{k}(A)$ does not hold, then the algorithm may simply fail.

In the first case of the proof of Lemma 3.4, the set $A$ satisfies that $T_{k-1}(A)\geq|A|^{2(k-1)-1-c+\delta}$ , for some constant $\delta$ . Without knowing if this previous condition is actually satisfied, we regardless call the algorithm recursively for $k-1$ . If it reports $H$ as claimed, then we are done. Otherwise, we can infer that we instead in the second case.

In that second case, we construct sets $Q_{D}$ approximating the sets $P_{D}$ from the proof of Lemma 3.4 as follows. Here, $D$ ranges of all powers of $2$ at least $|A|^{k-1-c-o(1)}$ . Each set $Q_{D}$ is required to satisfy that (i) each $x\in Q_{D}$ has multiplicity at least $D/2$ and less than $4D$ as a $k$ -sum in $A$ and (ii) each $k$ -sum in $A$ with multiplicity at least $D$ and less than $2D$ is contained in $Q$ . Each such set $Q_{D}$ can be computed in time $\tilde{O}(|A|^{1+c})$ by a constant number of calls to Lemma 3.3. Then, by the same proof as in Lemma 3.4 we have that

$$ T_{k}(A)\leq O((k\log|A|)^{2})\cdot\max_{D}(D^{2}\cdot E(A,Q_{D})), $$

and thus

$$ E(A,Q_{D})\geq\frac{|A|^{2}|Q_{D}|}{|A|^{\delta+o(1)}} $$

for some choice of $D$ . In this case we apply the asymmetric BSG theorem on $A$ and $Q_{D}$ . In the algorithm, we do not know the optimal value of $D$ , so we simply try all $O(\log|A|)$ options.
